paragraphs.text: An iron cake, or tie bing, of [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) from Yunnan, made in 1997 and pressed with a hydraulic press rather than in a stone mould. The press packs the leaf far harder and denser than stone does, and that density slows the cake’s ageing, so the outside of the cake changes faster than its heart.

It comes from the style’s third decade, twenty-four years after the [wet-pile method](shou:wet-piling) reached production in 1973. At twenty-nine years the cake counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged), where storage shapes it as much as the years do.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
